label: Machine Learning Through Geometry
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 231 through 278 and rereads familiar learning algorithms as moves on manifolds of distributions. Clustering, support vectors, message passing, and Boltzmann machines all become projections or metric-aware paths, so the geometry decides the shape of each update rather than the loss alone.

label: Algorithms as Projections
notes: The unifying claim is that a learning step is a projection of a data point or empirical distribution onto a model family. Whether the projection is exponential or mixture decides which Pythagorean relation holds, and that choice governs uniqueness, monotonic descent, and the geometry of every algorithm in this chapter.

label: Bregman Clustering
notes: Bregman divergences generalize squared distance while keeping the mean as the optimal center. Hard clustering alternates assigning each point to its nearest divergence center and recomputing centers as right-sided Bregman averages, which is an m-projection. The squared-Euclidean special case recovers ordinary k-means and Voronoi cells.

label: Divergence Centers and Voronoi
notes: With a Bregman divergence the decision boundary between two centers stays an affine hyperplane, so the partition is a genuine Voronoi tessellation. The notebook surface plots the nearest-center cost and checks that every point's assignment matches its true label, confirming the centers behave as stable divergence representatives.

label: Support Vectors as Margin Geometry
notes: A support-vector machine maximizes the margin, the gap between the separating hyperplane and the closest points. Only the support vectors touching the margin determine the solution. Geometrically the classifier is the perpendicular bisector geometry of the two convex hulls of the labeled point clouds.

label: Kernels and Feature Geometry
notes: A kernel computes inner products in a feature space without mapping points explicitly. The Gram matrix must be positive semidefinite, which makes it a valid metric on the data. The notebook checks the smallest eigenvalue stays nonnegative, certifying the induced feature-space geometry is well posed.

label: Graphical Models and Projection
notes: Belief propagation and mean-field both approximate an intractable distribution by projecting onto a tractable family. Mean-field performs an e-projection onto independent factorizations, minimizing reversed divergence, while loopy belief propagation seeks a stationary point of the Bethe free energy. Both are projection algorithms in disguise.

label: Mean-Field and Message Passing
notes: On a small factor graph each message is a normalized vector summarizing a neighbor's influence. The product of incoming messages with the local potential gives the belief, renormalized to a distribution. The notebook verifies every message and belief sums to one, the invariant that keeps the projection on the simplex.

label: Boosting as Dual Projection
notes: Boosting alternates two projections. The m-step reweights examples so the current model's expectations match the data, an m-projection onto a constraint surface. The e-step adds a weak learner, an e-projection onto the expanded model. AdaBoost is exactly this e- and m-projection cycle on the exponential family.

label: AdaBoost Reweighting
notes: Each AdaBoost round computes a weak learner's weighted error, sets its coefficient from the log-odds of that error, and reweights examples by an exponential factor before renormalizing. The notebook confirms the weights sum to one and the coefficient stays positive whenever the learner beats chance, matching the dual-projection picture.

label: Restricted Boltzmann Machines
notes: A restricted Boltzmann machine is a bipartite energy model whose visible and hidden layers carry no within-layer edges, so each conditional factorizes. The model defines an exponential family over binary states, and learning moves its parameters to reduce the divergence between the data distribution and the model marginals.

label: Contrastive Divergence
notes: Maximum likelihood for a Boltzmann machine needs the model expectation, which is intractable. Contrastive divergence approximates the gradient with a short Gibbs chain, so the update is the data moment minus a model moment. The notebook records that this difference has the expected sign, the geometric direction of the learning path.

label: Divergence-Based Learning
notes: Across the chapter every algorithm reduces a divergence between data and model along a metric-aware path. The Fisher metric reshapes gradients into natural gradients that follow short routes through parameter space, avoiding the singular valleys where ordinary Euclidean descent crawls slowly and ill-conditioned directions dominate.

label: Recap and Habits
notes: Leave with three habits. First identify the geometric object an algorithm represents. Second name the divergence or metric that decides the update's shape. Third pair every visual claim with a numerical invariant: positive eigenvalues, normalized messages, descending objectives. These habits transfer to models too large to draw directly.
